summary: Describes an implementation of music on hold in SIP that complies with standards, is effective, and avoids odd user interface effects. It is an informational service example.

eli5.summary: When you are waiting on the phone, music plays. This explains the right way to do it.

questions: how to implement music on hold
how to implement music on hold in sip
how does call hold work in sip
subtitle: A standards-compliant way to play music while holding a call in SIP.

tldr.problem: When one party to a SIP call places the call on hold, they want to provide audio (typically music) to the other party, but SIP's architecture makes this difficult to do while staying standards-compliant.
tldr.mechanism: The holding party sends a re-INVITE without SDP to force the remote party to provide an offer, then uses that offer to establish a separate call to a music source, which streams directly to the remote party.
tldr.outcome: The call is put on hold with music playing to the remote party, avoiding the user interface glitches and authentication issues of previous approaches. When the call is taken off hold, the music stops and normal bidirectional media resumes.

facts.label: Dialogs required
facts.value: Two: one to remote party, one to music source

today: RFC 7088 is Informational and describes a standard implementation practice. It remains valid as a recommended way to implement music on hold in SIP systems.

sections.title: Music on Hold in SIP
sections.content: Music on hold is a common feature in business telephone systems that provides audio to a caller while the call is on hold. In the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), a newer standard for voice calls over the Internet, implementing this feature is architecturally challenging. The RFC describes a method that is fully standards-compliant and avoids the quirks and failures of simpler approaches.
sections.eli5: When you call someone and they put you on hold, you hear music instead of silence. This document explains how to make that work correctly.

sections.title: How It Works: The SDP Offer Trick
sections.content:
The core of the technique revolves around the Session Description Protocol (SDP), which describes the audio formats and addresses both parties will use. When the holding party (the executing user agent) places a call on hold, it sends a re-INVITE without an SDP offer. This forces the remote party to provide an SDP offer in the response, which gives listening address and port information. The executing UA then uses that offer to initiate a call to an external music-on-hold source with the remote party's listening address, so the music streams directly to them.

The executing UA maintains two dialogs: one with the remote party and one with the music source. The music arrives at the remote party from the music source, not through the executing UA, reducing the load on the executing UA and avoiding network congestion.
sections.eli5: Imagine you want to forward music to someone. You ask them where they want it sent, then you tell the music machine their address so it sends directly to them.

sections.title: Message Sequences and Payload Type Handling
sections.content:
The technique involves a specific sequence of SIP messages. The executing UA sends a re-INVITE to the remote party with the +sip.rendering="no" field parameter in the Contact header to indicate the call is on hold. The remote party responds with SDP. The executing UA then sends an INVITE to the music source, uses the remote party's SDP offer, and modifies directionality to recvonly since the remote party will only receive. The music source responds with its own SDP answer.

A subtle problem arises with payload type numbers, which identify audio formats in SDP. The music source may reuse payload type numbers differently than before. The RFC specifies a solution: the executing UA can reserve payload type numbers by adding dummy entries to the offer sent to the music source, ensuring the music source will not reuse those numbers for different codecs.
sections.eli5: The parties exchange messages to agree on who sends what and how to label the audio format. Sometimes the number labels for audio formats can get mixed up, so the RFC explains how to prevent that.

sections.title: Taking the Call off Hold
sections.content:
When the user wants to resume the call, the executing UA sends a new re-INVITE to the remote party with SDP that requests normal bidirectional media. This removes the +sip.rendering="no" parameter from the Contact header. Once the remote party accepts, the executing UA sends a BYE request to the music source to terminate that dialog. Normal RTP media flow resumes between the two parties.

The executing UA must be prepared for other re-INVITEs during the hold state (from the remote party or the music source, for example to support ICE negotiation), which it handles by passing messages through, modifying SDP as needed.
sections.eli5: When you want to un-hold the call, you tell the music machine to stop and tell the other person they can talk to you again.

sections.title: Advantages Over Previous Methods
sections.content: This technique has several advantages. The original dialog remains unchanged, so the remote endpoint's user interface continues showing the original caller's identity instead of the music server's address. It does not require out-of-dialog REFER requests, which are not well-routed in all SIP systems. The music is sent directly from the source to the remote party, reducing computational load on the executing UA and avoiding "hairpinning" of media through network links. The remote party sees in SDP the address from which music will come, allowing it to accept the music even if it filters incoming media based on source address. The technique requires only simple SDP manipulation and does not require converting an SDP answer into an offer, unlike earlier proposals.
sections.eli5: This method is better than older ways because it is simpler, more reliable, does not confuse the caller about who they are calling, and does not overload the phone doing the holding.
